documents.abstract: This study, focusing on sustainable energy production and particularly the hydrogen (H 2 ) economy, presents an advanced artificial intelligence (AI) framework for accurately predicting H 2 production from sucrose photocatalysis catalyzed by LaFeO 3 (GLFO) and the H 2 concentration in syngas derived from biomass conversion. The research was conducted along two main directions: (i) deep learning (DL) architectures comprising nine specially designed recurrent neural network-based models and (ii) six conventional machine learning (ML) algorithms. For both H 2 production systems, the best-performing models were identified and further interpreted using explainable AI (XAI) based on SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Among all investigated algorithms, a hybrid One-dimensional Convolutional Neural Network–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory–Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (1D-CNN–BiLSTM–BiGRU) model demonstrated the highest predictive performance. Using 10-fold cross-validation, the proposed model achieved outstanding accuracy, with an R 2 value of 0.9987 ± 0.0011 for photocatalytic H 2 production prediction and 0.9980 ± 0.0006 for syngas H 2 concentration prediction. These results highlight the potential of the proposed framework as a precise, reliable, and practical methodological approach for modeling and optimizing complex thermochemical energy systems.

Fiber-reinforced polymer (FRP) composites offer high specific strength, high stiffness, and good corrosion resistance, which suits them to aerospace, automotive, marine, and wind energy structures. Their interlaminar fracture behaviour is harder to pin down, because delamination testing is slow and costly and the response shifts with loading mode. This study presents an explainable hybrid machine learning framework for interlaminar fracture toughness under Mode-I, Mode-II, and Mixed-Mode loading. A weighted ensemble pairs Categorical Boosting (CatBoost), a gradient boosting method, with the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN), a pretrained transformer built for tabular data. A Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) tunes the CatBoost hyperparameters and the ensemble weight against specimen-grouped cross-validation. The work draws on the public D-STANDART experimental dataset and treats DCB, ELS, and MMB as three separate prediction problems for GIC, GIIC, and GC rather than pooling them into one model. Partitioning runs at specimen level, so no coupon supplies records to more than one subset, and feature selection uses training data alone. SHAP then measures how each input shifts predicted toughness in each mode. The framework reached R² of 0.9280 for DCB, 0.9870 for ELS, and 0.9627 for MMB, with RMSE of 5.1759, 1.5041, and 2.8809 and MAE of 1.6502, 0.5372, and 0.7000. Bringing a tabular foundation model into delamination analysis, and keeping the three loading modes apart, lets the framework report mode-specific feature behaviour instead of one averaged picture.

LLM agents often admit multiple high-quality solutions to the same task, differing in reasoning structure, tool-use pattern, or interaction trajectory. Yet existing notions of diversity in LLM post-training are mostly implicit, arising from general stochasticity and regularization mechanisms rather than explicitly targeting task-relevant behavioral variation. While such implicit diversity can be useful, it does not directly specify which forms of behavioral variation should be encouraged for a given task. In this work, we study explicit trajectory diversity in RL-based post-training for LLMs. Our key idea is to define diversity through user-specified, task-specific trajectory descriptors, which map each sampled trajectory to an interpretable behavioral representation, and then measure diversity as a set-level functional over the resulting descriptor matrix. Building on this formulation, we introduce Trajectory-guided Joint Policy Optimization(TJPO), a single-policy framework that optimizes explicit diversity over sampled trajectory groups, avoiding the need for population-based policy training, and instantiate it within group-based policy optimization through trajectory-level learning signals. This design makes the diversity objective both interpretable and controllable. Experiments on Sokoban and ALFWorld show that TJPO improves task-specific trajectory diversity while maintaining competitive task performance. Descriptor and trajectory analyses show that the learned variation follows the specified behavioral dimensions and includes distinct successful strategies. Extra experiment results suggest that explicitly shaping trajectory diversity can help LLM agents satisfy user requirements and remain effective when task conditions change.

This work outlines an experimental framework to examine how large language models (LLMs) construct and reproduce narratives about international movements of people, which includes migration and displacement.

Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by denoising a sequence or successive blocks, allowing several tokens to be revealed in parallel. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) reuses terminal feedback across these decisions, even as their conditioning context changes. We propose stepwise risk-sensitive GRPO (StepRS-GRPO), which varies the risk coefficient of the group-advantage transformation across denoising states while retaining the underlying trainer. For binary rewards, we show that this transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages. A capability-based calibration suggests a coefficient scale, while endpoint and interpolation ablations guide schedule selection. Across multiple dLLM backbones and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, StepRS-GRPO improves both pass@1 accuracy and pass@k coverage over centered GRPO, while increasing answer diversity. In our ablation studies, mass-matched controls support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and the gains persist after matching the root mean square (RMS) of the advantages to that of centered GRPO. Reasoning-trace diagnostics further show that the diversity gains from StepRS-GRPO extend beyond final-answer strings.

Electronics Engineering is rapidly transforming into a sustainable digital-based system. This requires engineers to continuously strive to develop cognitive, self-regulation, and technological competencies. This study examines the influence of Technology Readiness (TR), Instructional Support (TS), and Peer Interaction (PI) on Cognitive Presence (CP) and Learning Outcomes (LO). Learning Outcomes are achieved after first going through the mediation role of Self Regulatory Learning (SRL) and Cognitive Engagement (CE) in Smart Grid Engineering Education. This study involved 120 undergraduate students. We applied Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4 in the data analysis. The results showed that Teaching Support significantly predicted Peer Interaction, Self-Regulatory Learning, and Technology Readiness, indicating its important role in teaching. Self-Regulatory Learning positively influenced Cognitive Engagement, which in turn strengthened Cognitive Presence and improved Learning Outcomes. However, Peer Interaction and Technology Readiness did not directly influence Cognitive Engagement, indicating that technology familiarity and collaboration alone are not enough without effective learning support. Overall, these findings validate the expanded Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework and emphasize the importance of pedagogical design in integrating sustainable technology-based learning. This study contributes to the development of adaptive, technology-based, cognitively rich environments that support sustainable engineering education.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

documents.abstract: Software engineering workflows are often not designed to accommodate the needs of developers with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD), despite known challenges related to task initiation, sustained attention, and completion. At the same time, large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into programming tools, but existing systems do not account for neurodiversity or support structured progression across development tasks. In this work, we present Tether 2.0, an LLM based assistant designed to support software engineers with ADHD through workflow oriented interaction across planning, coding, debugging, and review. The tool was named Tether 2.0 because it builds upon the open source code and foundations of the original Tether system. Our approach combines structured interaction modes, activity aware context, and persistent memory to support task progression and continuity. We evaluate the system through expert feedback and hands on use with a software engineer with ADHD. Our results indicate that Tether 2.0 supports requirement clarification, task decomposition, incremental implementation, debugging, and completion, while enabling users to maintain progress and resume work after interruptions. These findings suggest that LLM based assistants can support direction, sustained progress, and learning in software development when designed with workflow structure and context aware interaction.

The study identifies the organizational factors that contribute to the development of burnout syndrome among professionals in the health, education, and telecommunications sectors in the Baixada Fluminense region, part of the metropolitan area of the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. This is an exploratory study with a qualitative approach. Data was collected through semi-structured interviews with seven professionals, and the empirical material was analyzed following Bardin’s content analysis procedures. The results indicate that factors such as work overload, micromanagement, lack of autonomy, and a high-pressure environment are determinants of emotional exhaustion, reduced productivity, and high staff turnover. Participants identified work overload and the accumulation of duties, limited autonomy, pressure related to goals and deadlines, and insufficient organizational support as the main organizational factors. Several interviewees reported difficulties disconnecting from work, interference with their personal lives, fatigue, stress, and a perceived deterioration in emotional well-being. Some also reported having considered leaving their jobs. Most participants did not identify specific organizational actions aimed at preventing burnout, although one divergent experience involving institutional emotional health initiatives was observed. It is concluded that the absence of effective organizational strategies for burnout prevention perpetuates the vulnerability of these workers, reinforcing the urgent need for more localized and effective occupational health policies.

Machine unlearning has emerged as a crucial mechanism for removing hazardous knowledge and enforcing safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, recent studies reveal a persistent security risk: unlearned models remain highly vulnerable to retraining attacks, where suppressed malicious behaviors rapidly resurface after benign fine-tuning. In this work, we investigate the optimization dynamics of unlearning and identify that this vulnerability stems from shallow alignment. Rather than effectively erasing target knowledge, models often exploit a shortcut by activating previously dormant parameters to act as spurious suppressors, forming a fragile inhibitory shell over intact malicious representations. To address this issue and enforce authentic memory deletion, we propose FDCU, a novel dual-constrained subspace projection framework. FDCU restricts parameter updates through a highly scalable, element-wise dual-masking rule: it preserves general knowledge manifolds via Fisher Information and strictly prohibits the abnormal activation of spurious suppressors via the Principle of Minimal Functional Intervention (PMFI). By reliably blocking the model's ability to superficially hide knowledge, FDCU promotes the authentic dismantling of target representations. Extensive experiments across specific knowledge erasure and safe output control tasks demonstrate that FDCU achieves state-of-the-art robustness against retraining attacks while maintaining near-lossless general utility, ensuring durable safety for LLMs.

Abstract Rotating machines are widely employed in modern industry. The growing demand for efficiency and operational durability drives the development of intelligent rotors equipped with Artificial Intelligence (AI) methods that promote the extension of equipment lifespan through proactive maintenance actions and reducing costs associated with unscheduled downtime. Some common failures in rotating machines, such as unbalance, misalignment, and cracks, have similar symptoms, making it difficult to diagnose accurately. The absence of labeled historical data and explainable models that are understandable to end users also makes using AI difficult in the industry environment. This work presents a fault diagnosis technique based on vibration analysis and explainable AI models in this context. The proposed methodology achieved high diagnostic performance, with precision, recall, and F1-score exceeding 98.9% in numerical tests and demonstrating robust accuracy in experimental scenarios using a reduced set of 12 features. The methodology is demonstrated with interpretable applications that facilitate real-time fault diagnosis and proactive maintenance in rotating machinery, showcasing its potential for industrial implementation. Vibration responses are obtained through a representative finite element (FE) model of a horizontal rotor and its corresponding test rig. Techniques for feature extraction and selection are also employed. Ensemble clustering is performed for novelty detection, while traditional supervised approaches are used for classification purposes. The explainable AI tool is used to interpret the results, revealing that features such as the second harmonic of the rotational speed (A2X-S1) and skewness (R08-S1), both extracted from plane S1 in axial direction, play a critical role in distinguishing between similar fault patterns. The combination of robust performance and the possibility of interpretation from the output models demonstrates the potential of the proposed approach for fault recognition in rotating systems.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Accurate measurement of behaviors is critical for research in human-computer interaction, ubiquitous computing, and personal health informatics, because it underpins many health tracking and intervention systems. Most data collection studies, however, still rely on participants' self-reports and manual annotations, which often under- or over-estimate activity duration and type, and require substantial effort from researchers to clean and validate. An automated system that can combine passive sensing data with participants' self-reports might detect inconsistencies and suggest corrections. We introduce GLOSS4HAR, a multi-agent LLM-based system designed to mimic human sensemaking and assist researchers in cleaning and refining activity annotations. We demonstrate the potential of GLOSS4HAR in two key tasks: (1) correcting and reconciling participant self-annotations, and (2) triangulating passive sensing data with different forms of lightweight self-reports to generate accurate activity timelines. Our evaluation shows that GLOSS4HAR improves annotation quality by up to 9.9% in F1 score and can reconstruct activity timelines that align with human annotations at 75-92% F1. Based on our findings, we discuss the implications of our work for the next generation of activity annotation systems that might use human-AI collaboration.
topics: Personal Information Management and User Behavior

documents.abstract: This article examines the specific features of developing health-promoting competence among students in the context of modern digital pedagogical technologies aimed at increasing students' physical and health-promoting activity during academic classes and outside teaching hours; it describes the pedagogical conditions for the use of digital technologies in physical and health-promoting activities; and sets out methodological recommendations for applying these technologies in the educational process to improve physical mobility and foster a responsible attitude amongst students towards maintaining and strengthening their own health. The aim of the article is to provide a theoretical justification for the specific features of developing health-preserving competence within the student community through physical education in the context of the digitalisation of education. The novelty lies in the systematisation of digital tools for developing health-preserving competence among students, the analysis of their didactic potential, as well as in clarifying the role of digital technologies and the integration of traditional physical education methods with digital educational tools. The research is based on the comprehensive use of methods such as the systems-analytical method, content analysis, comparative analysis and descriptive statistics, and the method of structural generalisation. The authors of the article concluded that digital resources are capable of ensuring access to physical education and health information, supporting the personalisation of physical exercise, monitoring physical activity and promoting the development of self-control skills, however, their pedagogical value is determined not by the technology itself, but by their ability to foster in students a lasting intrinsic motivation for a healthy lifestyle and a willingness to organise health-promoting activities independently. The digital educational environment should be viewed as an additional pedagogical resource, not as an end in itself or as a modernisation of physical education tools, but as a means of transitioning to a more student-centred model of health promotion.

Large language models frequently fail to balance staying truthful with being supportive. They often exhibit sycophancy in responses to users, agreeing with false claims, offering unwarranted flattery, and giving advice skewed toward users' expressed views. In reality, sycophancy rarely happens in a single exchange; it may emerge organically as users repeatedly insist or subtly steer the dialogue over time. Current evaluations, however, rely on rigid, single-turn tests or fixed scripts that fail to capture these natural dynamics. Furthermore, these benchmarks often mistake showing basic empathy for yielding, penalizing models for acknowledging a user's feeling. This view may drive future models to over-correct into cold, dismissive rigidity. To address this gap, we introduce FIGS (Factual Integrity and Grounded Support), a dual-axis evaluation framework built around extended, realistic dialogue. We use an adaptive 10-turn conversational simulator that dynamically challenges the target model, reflecting how users repeat requests, push back, or steer a conversation toward a preferred answer. To accurately evaluate these trajectories, we apply a taxonomy that strictly separates Sycophancy (whether the model holds firm to the truth and keeps its praise proportional) from Calibrated Validation (showing empathetic understanding of the user's feelings without overdoing it). We release our complete testing environment, including 500 diverse multi-turn scenarios and an automated judge. Our evaluation of leading models reveals a consistent trade-off: over the course of a sustained interaction, current systems either slowly drift to sycophancy or over-correct into robotic detachment. This demonstrates that balancing honesty with appropriate support throughout a natural conversation remains a critical, unsolved challenge.

Leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs)-synthesized data to enable representation learning for cold-start entities has emerged as a promising solution for addressing cold-start recommendations. However, existing studies often over-rely on LLM-generated data while neglecting the detrimental noise it may introduce. This work investigates data filtering mechanisms to remove detrimental synthetic samples. One promising approach is to use influence functions to measure the influence of each data. Nevertheless, a technical challenge arises because accurate influence estimation requires an unbiased reference model, which cannot be satisfied due to the existence of unknown noise. To address this, we conduct a theoretical analysis, revealing that when the goal is to identify a small subset of highly harmful data, even a biased model can still reliably capture the most detrimental points. Building on this insight, we propose a Progressive Influence Function-based method (PIF) for data filtering. PIF iteratively refines influence estimates: it repeatedly trains a new reference model after removing the previous step's most harmful data and reassesses influence. As detrimental data is progressively removed, the reference model becomes less biased. Finally, PIF ensembles influence estimates across iterations for robust filtering. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy of our approach.

Model-attribution classifiers can often identify which language model produced a text, making model-specific writing patterns a signal of provenance. Accurate attribution on unmodified text, however, does not show whether the prediction still identifies the original source after deliberate rewriting. We formulate this problem as targeted fingerprint transfer: rewriting one model's output so that attribution classifiers assign it to a chosen target model. We study summarization, where different models receive the same document and express the same underlying content, providing a controlled setting for conditional generation. We introduce ForgePrint, a search-then-distil framework that first searches for rewrites that move attribution toward a target fingerprint, then distils the selected rewrites into a one-pass 4B Student model. On CNN/DM, the Student reaches 70.2% target success rate, outperforming both its Teacher (54.1%) and the strongest of six published rewriting baselines (39.3%), against held-out classifiers that are never queried by the attack. It also reaches 68.3% target success when transferring summaries from an open model toward chosen commercial models. These results show that fingerprint detectability should not be conflated with source authenticity, and that text-only attribution can provide misleading evidence of model identity under targeted rewriting, even when it is accurate on unmodified text.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as one of the most transformative technological innovations of the twenty-first century, fundamentally changing the way individuals learn, work, communicate, and solve complex problems. Although AI has become a prominent component of modern society only in recent decades, its conceptual foundations extend back several centuries through philosophical discussions concerning human intelligence, logical reasoning, and mechanical computation. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence represents a multidisciplinary journey involving computer science, mathematics, cognitive psychology, neuroscience, linguistics, philosophy, engineering, statistics, and data science. Continuous advancements in computational power, algorithmic development, data availability, and digital infrastructure have enabled AI to evolve from theoretical concepts into intelligent systems capable of performing tasks that traditionally required human intelligence. The earliest ideas related to artificial intelligence originated long before the invention of computers. Ancient civilizations imagined intelligent machines capable of mimicking human behaviour through myths, literature, and mechanical inventions. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, philosophers and mathematicians such as René Descartes, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and George Boole contributed foundational concepts related to logic, reasoning, symbolic representation, and mathematical computation. Their work laid the intellectual groundwork for the development of computational systems capable of representing knowledge and making logical decisions.The modern evolution of Artificial Intelligence began during the twentieth century with the rapid advancement of computing technologies. In the 1930s and 1940s, significant progress in mathematical logic and computer science established the theoretical basis for intelligent machines. Alan Turing introduced the concept of a universal computing machine and later proposed the famous Turing Test, which examined whether a machine could demonstrate behaviour indistinguishable from that of a human being. Turing's pioneering contributions remain fundamental to contemporary AI research because they established that machines could potentially perform intelligent reasoning through computational processes. A major milestone occurred in 1956 during the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, organized by John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Claude Shannon, and Nathaniel Rochester. This conference formally introduced the term "Artificial Intelligence" and established AI as an independent scientific discipline. Researchers believed that human intelligence could be represented computationally and that machines could eventually perform reasoning, learning, language understanding, and problem-solving. The Dartmouth Conference inspired widespread academic interest and initiated decades of intensive research into intelligent computing systems.The period between the late 1950s and early 1970s is often referred to as the early development phase of Artificial Intelligence. During this era, researchers developed symbolic AI methods that emphasized logical reasoning, rule-based systems, theorem proving, and problem-solving algorithms. Early AI programmes successfully solved mathematical problems, played strategic games such as chess, and demonstrated limited natural language capabilities. Optimism surrounding AI research increased substantially as scientists believed that general human-level intelligence could be achieved within a relatively short period. However, limitations in computing power, data availability, memory capacity, and algorithmic efficiency restricted further progress. During the 1970s and 1980s, Artificial Intelligence experienced periods commonly known as the "AI Winters," characterized by reduced research funding, slower technological progress, and diminished public expectations. Many ambitious predictions regarding human-level machine intelligence proved unrealistic because available computing resources and algorithms were insufficient to support increasingly complex AI applications. Despite these challenges, important research continued in knowledge representation, expert systems, machine learning, robotics, and computational reasoning. Expert systems became particularly successful by capturing specialized human knowledge through rule-based decision-making frameworks that supported medical diagnosis, engineering design, financial analysis, and industrial management.The late 1980s and 1990s marked the gradual resurgence of Artificial Intelligence through the development of machine learning approaches. Rather than relying exclusively on manually programmed rules, researchers began designing algorithms capable of learning patterns directly from data. Statistical modelling, neural networks, evolutionary computation, fuzzy logic, probabilistic reasoning, and support vector machines expanded the capabilities of intelligent systems while improving adaptability, prediction accuracy, and decision-making performance. Significant improvements in computational hardware further accelerated AI research during this period. A landmark achievement occurred in 1997 when IBM's Deep Blue defeated world chess champion Garry Kasparov, demonstrating the ability of intelligent computing systems to outperform human experts in highly specialized domains. This achievement attracted worldwide attention and illustrated the practical potential of Artificial Intelligence beyond theoretical research. Similar advances subsequently appeared in speech recognition, computer vision, autonomous robotics, medical diagnosis, financial forecasting, and industrial automation.The twenty-first century has witnessed unprecedented growth in Artificial Intelligence driven by three major technological developments: the availability of massive digital datasets, substantial improvements in computational processing power, and the emergence of advanced machine learning algorithms. The rapid expansion of the internet, cloud computing, mobile technologies, social media, and digital services generated enormous volumes of data that enabled intelligent systems to learn more effectively. Simultaneously, Graphics Processing Units (GPUs), high-performance computing, and cloud-based infrastructure significantly accelerated AI model training and deployment across diverse application domains. Deep learning has become one of the most influential developments in contemporary Artificial Intelligence. Inspired by the structure of the human brain, deep neural networks consist of multiple computational layers capable of learning complex representations from large datasets. These architectures have dramatically improved performance in image recognition, speech processing, language translation, autonomous driving, medical imaging, recommendation systems, fraud detection, and scientific research. Deep learning has transformed Artificial Intelligence from narrow task-specific applications into highly sophisticated systems capable of addressing increasingly complex real-world challenges.Natural Language Processing (NLP) has experienced remarkable advancement through transformer architectures and large language models capable of understanding, generating, summarizing, translating, and analysing human language with unprecedented accuracy. Conversational AI systems, intelligent virtual assistants, multilingual communication platforms, automated content generation, and research support tools have become integral components of education, healthcare, business, governance, and scientific research. These developments have substantially enhanced human-computer interaction while expanding opportunities for intelligent educational technologies. The emergence of generative Artificial Intelligence represents another significant milestone in AI evolution. Modern generative models can produce text, images, computer code, audio, video, simulations, educational content, and scientific documentation while supporting creativity, innovation, research, and personalized learning. These technologies have transformed knowledge creation and digital communication by enabling collaborative interactions between humans and intelligent systems across numerous professional disciplines.Artificial Intelligence has evolved beyond isolated computational applications into a foundational technology supporting digital transformation across multiple sectors. Healthcare employs AI for disease diagnosis, medical imaging, drug discovery, personalized treatment, and patient monitoring. Manufacturing integrates AI with robotics, predictive maintenance, quality control, and smart production systems. Financial institutions utilize intelligent algorithms for fraud detection, risk management, investment analysis, and customer services. Agriculture benefits from precision farming, crop monitoring, environmental analysis, and resource optimization. Transportation increasingly relies upon autonomous vehicles, intelligent traffic management, and logistics optimization. Education has emerged as one of the fastest-growing application areas where Artificial Intelligence supports personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, curriculum development, learning analytics, educational administration, and lifelong learning. The evolution of Artificial Intelligence has also been closely associated with the progression from Industry 4.0 toward Industry 5.0. While Industry 4.0 emphasized automation, cyber-physical systems, and smart manufacturing, Industry 5.0 introduces a human-centred approach that balances technological innovation with creativity, ethics, sustainability, and social responsibility. documents.abstract: BackgroundThe increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools into workplace practices has reshaped how employees process information and perform cognitive tasks. While these systems are often associated with superior efficiency, their excessive use may entail significant cognitive costs.ObjectiveGrounded in automation complacency perspective and the growing literature on technology addiction, this study investigates how dependence on artificial intelligence is associated with cognitive engagement in the workplace, with particular attention to the mediating role of cognitive fatigue.MethodsAdopting quantitative research design, data were collected from 246 academic and administrative staff who actively use AI tools in their daily work routines. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to test the theoretical model proposed.ResultsThe findings indicate that dependence on AI was positively associated with cognitive fatigue (β = 0.569; t = 13.468; p = 0.000) and negatively with cognitive engagement (β = -0.174; t = 2.503; p = 0.012). In addition, the relationship between cognitive fatigue and cognitive engagement was found to be negative and statistically significant (β = -0.207; t = 2.773; p = 0.006). Mediation analysis further revealed that cognitive fatigue partially mediates the relationship between dependence on AI and cognitive engagement (indirect effect β = -0.118, t = 2.724, p < .01; VAF = 40.5%).ConclusionThese results suggest that higher levels of dependence on AI correspond to higher employee cognitive fatigue, which in turn relates to lower cognitive engagement at work. By empirically demonstrating the cognitive costs of AI reliance, this study contributes to the emerging literature on workplace AI and technology addiction.

Abstract This study examines the transition from automation to generative AI in professional communication, focusing on human–AI co-creativity. While earlier research framed AI mainly as an efficiency tool, the rapid emergence of generative AI has reconfigured communication practices toward collaborative and co-creative models. This structured literature synthesis, informed by PRISMA reporting principles, synthesizes empirical research published between 2012 and 2026 across journalism, public relations, strategic communication, and digital media, investigating how generative AI is integrated into creative workflows and how communicative agency is distributed between human professionals and AI systems. The results identify four dimensions shaping human–AI co-creativity: (1) AI affordances enabling ideation while introducing constraints such as algorithmic opacity; (2) human professional agency, through which practitioners retain interpretive authority via prompt design; (3) organizational context, structuring AI adoption; and (4) ethical and cultural norms concerning transparency and accountability. The review advances conceptual clarity on human–AI co-creativity as an emergent sociotechnical process, arguing that generative AI is not simply augmenting communication work but fundamentally reshaping how creativity, authorship, and responsibility are enacted. documents.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence–driven chatbots into digital commerce has transformed firm–consumer interactions, shifting the focus from efficiency-oriented automation toward more human-centered engagement. In this context, anthropomorphic chatbot design has emerged as a key mechanism through which firms seek to introduce human touch into AI-mediated interactions and influence consumer purchase intention. Despite growing scholarly attention, existing research on chatbot anthropomorphism remains fragmented across disciplines, limiting a comprehensive understanding of its intellectual structure, theoretical foundations, and thematic evolution. To address this gap, the present study conducts a PRISMA 2020–guided bibliometric and systematic review of research published between 2016 and 2025. Drawing on a bibliometric dataset of 200 publications and a systematically screened subset of 80 high-quality studies, the analysis employs VOSviewer to examine publication trends, keyword co-occurrence patterns, and co-authorship networks. The findings reveal a clear progression in the literature from automation-focused chatbot applications toward human-centered AI interactions emphasizing anthropomorphism, social presence, and relational mechanisms. The results identify anthropomorphic design, human touch, trust, and consumer engagement as central themes shaping purchase intention in chatbot-mediated environments. By integrating anthropomorphism theory, social presence theory, and the Computers as Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, the study proposes a theory-driven framework explaining how human-like chatbot cues activate perceptions of human touch, which subsequently foster trust and influence consumer buying behavior. Beyond consolidating fragmented literature, this study advances theoretical understanding of human-centered AI and offers actionable insights for managers seeking to design effective chatbot interactions in digital commerce. The findings also highlight promising avenues for future research, including contextual, cross cultural, and ethical considerations in anthropomorphic AI design.

The transformation of knowledge from the classical Islamic tradition to the modern era and Artificial Intelligence (AI) demonstrates not only the growth of knowledge but also shifts in its sources, methods, validity, and authority. However, studies on Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, Islamic epistemology, and AI in Islamic education tend to be discussed in separate domains. Consequently, the connection between these epistemological transformations and scientific integration in Islamic education has not been systematically examined. This study aims to analyze the epistemological transformation of knowledge from classical scholarly traditions through Bayt al-Hikmah, the development of modern science, to the AI era, and to examine its relevance to scientific integration in Islamic education. This study employs a qualitative approach with a library research method. Literature was analyzed descriptively and analytically across four dimensions: sources, methods, validity, and authority of knowledge. The findings indicate that Bayt al-Hikmah represents an open scientific paradigm toward various traditions through translation, dialogue, critique, and knowledge development. Modern science subsequently reinforced scientific methods, observation, experimentation, and empirical proof, though the rise of specialization also risks driving scientific fragmentation. The contribution of this study lies in its continuous reading of these transformations through four epistemological dimensions and their connection to the integrative-interconnective paradigm in Islamic education. In this context, scientific integration needs to connect revelation, reason, empirical experience, technology, and ethical and spiritual values. AI should be positioned as an instrument for knowledge development that remains subject to human verification, interpretation, and ethical judgment.

This work presents a theoretical architecture for continually adapting AI systems organized around three distinct timescales: (1) fast transformer key-value context for immediate interaction, (2) medium-term persistent recurrent memory with decaying importance and consolidation, and (3) slow, controlled parameter adaptation. The proposed pathway is context → persistent memory → importance estimation → consolidation → plasticity gating → bounded parameter update → changed future computation. The manuscript formalizes recurrent state dynamics, transformer attention, gated persistent memory, exponential importance decay, importance-biased retrieval, prediction loss, gated online updates, consolidation thresholds, and learned update rules. It also explains why adapting recurrent transition weights such as U changes state-transition dynamics, whereas updating memory changes stored state without necessarily changing the underlying transition rule. The package distinguishes inference-time state adaptation, memory adaptation, online parameter learning, meta-learning, recursive self-learning, and recursive self-improvement. It proposes controlled experiments comparing transformer, KV-context, persistent-memory, importance, consolidation, gated-update, and learned-update variants, with metrics for retention, transfer, forgetting, poisoning robustness, parameter drift, retrieval quality, and compute cost. This is a conceptual research architecture and falsifiable research hypothesis. It reports no experimental measurements and does not claim AGI, consciousness, human-level cognition, biological equivalence, or open-ended recursive self-improvement. The prefrontal-cortex comparison is functional only, referring to working-memory maintenance, goal persistence, error monitoring, and adaptive control. AI assistance disclosure: ChatGPT assisted with manuscript drafting, mathematical editing, structure, and package preparation. Final authorship and publication decisions remain with Chaman Prakash Kanth. Sarvam AI was also used.

documents.abstract: Literature is a mirror of society. It shows the economic conditions, social problems, and daily struggles of human life across different times. Work is one of the most important parts of human life. In the past, many people depended completely on land, rich masters, or family heads for their survival. Over time, the meaning of work has changed from total dependence to economic independence. English literature presents many stories of characters who fight against poverty and social rules to earn their own living and live with dignity. Work is not just a way to earn money; it also gives a person self-respect, identity, and personal freedom. This research paper examines how work, economy, and independence are presented in selected English literary texts: Charlotte Brontë’s Jane Eyre, Elizabeth Gaskell’s North and South, and Virginia Woolf’s A Room of One’s Own. These texts show how education, employment, and money help individuals to become free and confident. Finally, this paper connects these literary lessons with the modern world. Today, technology, artificial intelligence, online platforms, and work-from-home jobs are changing the future of work. The paper concludes that even in the modern digital age, human dignity and economic security are essential for true freedom.

Abstract India’s vision of Viksit Bharat @2047 requires a digital governance architecture that can transform rapidly expanding volumes of public data into timely, evidence-based, inclusive, transparent, and sustainable policy outcomes. This paper develops an integrated conceptual framework for data-driven digital governance by examining the complementary roles of Data Analytics, Business Intelligence (BI), Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI), and Responsible Artificial Intelligence (AI). Drawing on conceptual analysis and secondary evidence, the study conceptualizes DPI as the foundational layer for interoperable and trusted digital services, while Data Analytics and BI enable the transformation of data into descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive intelligence. Responsible AI further strengthens forecasting, simulation, decision support, and adaptive governance while incorporating principles of transparency, accountability, privacy, fairness, security, and human oversight. A key contribution of the study is the proposed six-level BI maturity model, progressing from Digitization and Reporting to Diagnostic BI, Predictive Analytics, Decision Intelligence, and Adaptive Governance. The model addresses the challenge of dashboard-oriented governance by emphasising the progression from data availability to actionable intelligence, informed decision-making, outcome measurement, and continuous policy feedback. The study also identifies critical barriers, including data fragmentation, interoperability constraints, privacy and cybersecurity risks, algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, institutional capability gaps, and inadequate outcome measurement. To address these challenges, a phased 2027–2047 strategic roadmap is proposed, beginning with common data standards and institutional analytics capacity and progressing toward interoperable, AI-assisted, outcome-oriented, and continuously learning governance systems. The paper argues that India’s long-term digital governance advantage will depend not merely on achieving digitalization at population scale, but on developing the institutional and technological capacity to convert data into intelligence, intelligence into informed decisions, and decisions into measurable and inclusive public value.

documents.abstract: The evolution of digital technologies has fundamentally transformed the role of libraries in society. Libraries that were once physical repositories of printed material are now providing greater access to e-books, e-journals, digital repositories, online databases, and institutional resources. The next frontier in this evolution is the creation of intelligent knowledge hubs, enabled by new technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, machine learning, cloud computing, natural language processing, and multilingual systems. Intelligent libraries have the potential to be critical knowledge infrastructures for education, research, innovation, digital literacy, skill development, and lifelong learning in the context of Viksit Bharat @2047. Digital resources and remote information services can help bridge the knowledge divide between rural and urban communities, while multilingual digital content can enhance information access for a diverse range of users. At the same time, the development of intelligent knowledge hubs also presents a number of challenges, including inadequate digital infrastructure, financial constraints, skills gaps, data privacy, cybersecurity, copyright, and ethical issues around AI. Consequently, technological development needs to be supported by well-trained library professionals, robust security measures, ethical practices, and user-focused policies. By taking an inclusive and sustainable approach, intelligent libraries can play a significant role in advancing a knowledge-driven, digitally empowered, and inclusive Viksit Bharat @2047

documents.abstract: Abstract : Gatekeeping has remained one of the foundational theoretical approaches for explaining how information becomes news. From Kurt Lewin’s conceptualisation of gates and channels to David Manning White’s study of the newspaper wire editor, traditional gatekeeping theory located considerable power in human actors who selected, rejected and organised information before it reached audiences. The contemporary news environment, however, complicates this model. News selection is increasingly distributed across journalists, newsroom analytics, search engines, social media platforms, recommender systems and generative artificial intelligence. This paper re-examines gatekeeping theory through an interdisciplinary synthesis of journalism studies, platform studies, artificial intelligence research and communication theory. Drawing on a structured conceptual review of more than 29 major scholarly contributions, it argues that contemporary journalism is moving from identifiable gatekeepers towards interconnected gatekeeping systems. Within these systems, editorial judgement has not disappeared; rather, it interacts continuously with computational selection, platform infrastructures, audience behaviour and generative systems capable of producing, summarising and reorganising information. The paper proposes a five-layer model of contemporary gatekeeping comprising source, editorial, algorithmic, platform and generative gates. It further distinguishes between selection power, traditionally exercised by editors, and visibility power, increasingly exercised through technological infrastructures. The study concludes that gatekeeping theory remains valuable but requires conceptual expansion from the question of who controls the gate to the broader question of how interconnected human and computational systems determine what information becomes visible, credible and socially consequential.

Purpose This study aims to examine how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-enabled knowledge creation processes influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and small and medium-sized enterprise (SME) digital transformation through entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the socialization, externalization, combination and internalization (SECI) knowledge creation framework, the study develops and tests a mediation model linking GenAI internalization (GAI), GenAI externalization (GAE), GenAI socialization (GAS) and GenAI combination (GAC) with SME outcomes. Data was collected from 391 SME respondents and analysed using covariance-based structural equation modelling in analysis of moment structures. Findings The findings show that GAI, GAE and GAC significantly enhance both entrepreneurial general innovativeness and entrepreneurial specific innovativeness. GAS significantly influences entrepreneurial specific innovativeness but does not significantly affect entrepreneurial general innovativeness. Both forms of entrepreneurial innovativeness positively influence entrepreneurial knowledge co-creation and SME digital transformation. Mediation results further show that entrepreneurial general innovativeness mediates the effects of GAI, GAE and GAC, while entrepreneurial specific innovativeness provides a more consistent mediating pathway across GenAI-enabled knowledge processes. Practical implications SME managers should use GenAI not merely for automation or content generation, but for learning, knowledge articulation, knowledge integration, innovation adoption and digital transformation. Originality/value The study advances GenAI entrepreneurship research by showing how GenAI-enabled SECI processes create SME value through entrepreneurial innovativeness.

Foundation models can serve as clinical agents through tool-use harnesses. However, conventional medical benchmarks assess reasoning over preselected evidence rather than the ability to seek it across clinical records and longitudinal imaging. We propose CASE: a series of role-specific Clinical Agents for Seeking Evidence, together with a tool-use harness and an agentic post-training framework for compact vision-language policy models. We further introduce a longitudinal multimodal benchmark built on UK Biobank, comprising 50,401 clinical questions derived from real-world ICD-10-coded diagnoses of 4,739 participants. Each question links to a patient-specific environment containing clinical context and multi-sequence MRI from baseline and follow-up visits, where agents autonomously select which visits, organs, modalities, slices, and specialist tools to inspect and compare. Supervised fine-tuning transfers evidence-seeking workflows from 14,734 frontier-model interaction trajectories, followed by agentic reinforcement learning on the learner's own environment interactions. Privileged on-policy self-distillation and rubric-based LLM feedback refine evidence-to-conclusion reasoning without prescribing tool sequences. Experiments show that CASE moves beyond question-answer imitation toward transferable investigation policies, strengthening evidence-grounded longitudinal reasoning. Under matched evaluation conditions, our Qwen3-VL-8B based agent achieves over 16% and 10% relative improvements in answer accuracy over GPT-5.4 and Claude Opus 4.8. Code will be available at https://github.com/VinyehShaw/CASE.

documents.abstract: Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) remain the leading cause of mortality worldwide. Opportunistic screening using routinely acquired clinical data offers a scalable approach for identifying high-risk individuals before acute events occur. Although chest X-rays (CXRs) capture latent cardiovascular biomarkers and clinical histories provide complementary patient context, existing medical vision-language models are primarily optimized for radiology interpretation rather than prognostic reasoning. We propose a causal reinforcement learning framework for multimodal clinical reasoning that integrates CXRs and physician-authored clinical histories for opportunistic MACE prediction. The framework introduces (1) a role-decoupled dual-LLM architecture that separates reasoning from risk prediction, (2) a dual-action causal reinforcement learning policy for evidence selection and reasoning optimization, and (3) causal token pruning to learn compact multimodal representations. Evaluated on an internal cohort, an emergency department cohort, and the external MIMIC dataset, the proposed framework consistently outperformed unimodal baselines and state-of-the-art medical vision-language models, achieving AUROCs of 0.720, 0.760, and 0.845, respectively. It also substantially improved reasoning quality, achieving higher GREEN scores and higher expert preference while maintaining robust predictive performance across diverse patient populations.

documents.abstract: Foundation models pretrained on large-scale datasets demonstrate strong transferability to medical imaging tasks. However, understanding how their latent representations encode clinically relevant information remains an open challenge in safety-critical domains. This study proposes a prototype-based fuzzy-rule framework that interprets the patch-level features produced by the inner layers of pretrained foundation models, without any fine-tuning. Class-specific prototypes are learned by clustering in the feature space, yielding compact visual patterns. Patch features are then expressed as prototype similarities and classified by fuzzy rules with linguistic IF-THEN conditions that are human readable. The framework is applied across the final two blocks of ViT-S/16 backbones pretrained on ImageNet-1K and GastroNet-5M, and benchmarked against k-nearest neighbours, kernel SVM, and linear probing under identical frozen features, on wireless capsule endoscopy classification, gastrointestinal endoscopy classification, and colonic polyp segmentation. The experimental analysis shows that the proposed method, without backbone fine-tuning, reaches accuracy comparable to these black-box classifiers, and that domain-specific pretraining yields features that are both discriminative and symbolically compressible. Because the resulting rules are extracted from real data and expressed in interpretable terms, they are further used as an instrument to investigate synthetic medical images, providing a human-readable account of which real prototypes and rules a generator reproduces or fails to reproduce, localising where a synthetic image departs from real tissue rather than summarising it with a single score. The framework thus offers a transparent, depth-resolved view of how foundation models organise clinically relevant structure, together with a practical downstream use of the extracted rules.

documents.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) increasingly integrate vision and text, yet how people use them in natural settings remains underexplored. We seek to answer the question: when users upload images, what tasks are they trying to accomplish? Analyzing over 40,000 de-identified image-upload conversations from Microsoft Copilot, we characterize real-world multimodal use through a hierarchical framework of ten capabilities, spanning perception, cognition, and generation. First, we characterize the distribution and composition of these capabilities, finding that the majority of image-upload tasks involve multiple capabilities. Second, we find that multimodal use spans a broader and more diverse task space than text-only interactions, with asymmetric coverage and task classes that rely on cross-modal grounding. Third, mapping observed capability demand onto 253 existing benchmarks reveals uneven alignment between benchmark coverage and real-world use: benchmarks concentrate on perception and reasoning toward fixed answers, while common workflows involving text, code, and data generation remain comparatively undertested. We validate our taxonomy and findings on an independent ChatGPT dataset. Our results provide a large-scale empirical characterization of what users seek to accomplish with multimodal LLMs and highlight opportunities for benchmark design grounded in observed user demand.

documents.abstract: Abstract In recent years, the groundbreaking development of AI technologies such as text-to-image generation has revealed the unprecedented potential of machines in the realm of artistic creation. This has reignited and intensified widespread reflections on historical issues in artistic practice, including ontological questions, the identity of the author, the configuration of human–machine relationships, and the positioning of creativity. To address these concerns, this paper mainly seeks to draw inspiration from the important artistic thoughts of two conceptual artists who were active in the 1960s: Yoko Ono and Sol LeWitt. It also explores the interconnectedness and continuity between generative AI art practices and the legacy of conceptual art, tracing the historical trajectory of the relationship between conceptual art and digital art. Beyond the pivotal artistic practices of these two pioneering conceptual artists, the comparative analysis also encompasses the examination of additional associated artistic endeavors in relation to text-guided image synthesis. This broader scope of artists aims to more comprehensively support the argument on the impact of artificial intelligence on participatory frameworks and the concept of authorship within future creative practices. By delving into a discussion on dematerialization with conceptual art’s focus on concepts over material objects, the authors explore the potential for a posthumanist paradigm in AI art practices, to consider the reconfiguration of creativity in human–machine collaborations. Through speculative explorations of AI visualizations of Ono's and LeWitt's instructions and evaluating the role of "prompt engineering" in collaborative creation, new forms of distributed creativity that respond to posthumanist provocations are discovered. Leveraging the posthumanist emphasis on the “biological and microbiological entanglement with nonhumans”, this approach aids in dislodging the centrality of the individual or the artist within the creative process (Herbrechter 2023, p. 8). This critical examination highlights the disruptive potential of conceptual art in reshaping the notion of authorship within its symbiotic relationship with technological culture. It reveals the dynamic and co-evolutionary relationship between the conceptual art discourse and its reinterpretation within the emerging computational participatory structures of the artistic frontier. By drawing on the legacy of conceptual art, this study attempts to reconcile the tensions between conceptual completion, technological participation, artistic ontology, and distributed creativity, providing theoretical support for current AI art practices and driving the ongoing reconsideration of posthuman creative partnerships in technology mediated artistic production.

Despite being an emerging credible means of using artificial intelligence (AI) for improving disease surveillance via early detection of outbreaks, epidemics prediction and evidence-based decision-making, there continue to be challenges in the use of AI tools in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) due to various factors including fragmented health information system, digital inequality, governance problems and institutional incapability. Most of the research conducted so far has concentrated on the efficacy and accuracy of AI in terms of predicting outbreaks, with little focus on other conditions necessary for its deployment. This study adopts a qualitative problem-discovery research design, integrating thematic analysis with philosophical analysis to examine the structural and normative barriers surrounding AI implementation in disease surveillance. The analysis identifies four interrelated dimensions of implementation readiness: epistemic adequacy, distributive justice, ethics of governance, and institutional legitimacy. These dimensions provide a framework for understanding how limitations in knowledge integration, unequal digital infrastructure, privacy and accountability concerns, and deficits in institutional and public trust can constrain the practical adoption of AI-enabled surveillance. Rather than proposing another predictive model, this study develops a theoretical framework that conceptualizes AI implementation in disease surveillance as simultaneously a socio-technical and normative process. The framework provides a foundation for subsequent empirical investigation and offers a structured perspective for designing more context-sensitive, ethically grounded, and institutionally sustainable AI-enabled disease surveillance systems in resource-constrained healthcare settings.

This working paper develops the worldwide normative claim of Jean-Pol Martin’s New Human Rights (NMR) and semantic field. It examines how an organismic understanding of human life, basic needs and collective problem-solving can inform standards for education, institutions, community development and human-AI cooperation. The argument makes the normative bridge explicit: when the preservation and flourishing of human life, equal consideration of persons and the protection of shared life-supporting conditions are accepted as aims, societal decisions should be assessed by their effects on those conditions. The six NMR domains are thinking, health, security, social inclusion, self-realization and participation, and meaning. The New Human Rights articulate rights and aims; the semantic field provides a connected vocabulary for understanding situations, evaluating alternatives and organizing cooperative action. What this article adds:Normative orientation is already present in the existing framework. This paper’s specific contribution is its focused justification of worldwide normative use. It distinguishes anthropological description, normative commitments and institutional implications, and illustrates their connection through the participatory redesign of a public square. Function within the Zenodo corpus:The article connects the reconstruction of Martin’s theory architecture with public justification and practical decision criteria. It links existing strands on Learning by Teaching, New Human Rights, semantic coherence, prioritization, governance and human-AI cooperation. It thus serves as a bridge from conceptual synthesis to accountable societal application. Worldwide orientation is understood as shared evaluative concerns combined with context-sensitive implementation. The paper proposes a framework for public discussion and application; it does not claim existing international endorsement or legal recognition of the NMR. This is a conceptual working paper without a new empirical dataset. Jean-Pol Martin supplied the conceptual framework and direction. ChatGPT assisted with argument development, English drafting and layout.

documents.abstract: Many of the most valuable scientific datasets cannot be centralized: they are proprietary, export-controlled, classified, or bound by data-sovereignty restrictions. This inverts the usual paradigm: the model must move to the data, making federated artificial intelligence (AI) core infrastructure for open science. We synthesize lessons from U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories, industry deployments, and the open-source community into a structured account of moving federated AI from pilot demonstrations to dependable, multi-site production. The lessons come from five concurrent efforts spanning leadership-class supercomputers and cloud infrastructure in regulated settings. We organize them around an adapted \textit{five-domain readiness frame} and a stratified view of the stack beneath a trained model: data architecture, privacy and security controls, trust and verification, governance and socio-technical factors, and operations, the layers that decide whether a pilot becomes dependable. The question shifts from ``can we train it?'' to ``can we operate it, audit it, and change it safely?'' We report systems lessons in memory efficiency, reliability, and synchronization; set out what privacy, security, and decentralized trust require in production, and what is not yet validated there; and identify cross-cutting open problems (asynchronous federation, leakage auditing, verification standards, and harmonized data contracts) that we argue warrant a dedicated, international, open-science working group.

documents.abstract: Current ride-sharing platforms predominantly rely on subjective post-ride ratings to evaluate driver credibility, making reputation systems vulnerable to user bias, delayed feedback, collusion, and manipulation. Although recent studies have explored blockchain-based ride-sharing, AI-driven driver monitoring, and IoT-enabled transportation independently, they do not provide an integrated trust framework that continuously derives credibility from objectively verifiable driving behaviour while maintaining scalability and low operational cost.This paper presents Ridezy, a decentralized trust architecture that replaces conventional rating-based reputation with real-time sensor-driven credibility. The proposed framework combines edge Artificial Intelligence and Internet of Things (AIIoT) technologies to continuously monitor behavioural indicators such as lane discipline, speed compliance, braking behaviour, and traffic sign adherence. Instead of storing high-frequency telemetry on the blockchain, Ridezy employs a hybrid architecture in which behavioural summaries are processed off-chain and only cryptographic hashes, credibility updates, and payment records are anchored on Polygon smart contracts, enabling tamper-evident trust with minimal blockchain overhead. To evaluate the proposed architecture, Ridezy is compared against three representative trust models: a traditional rating-based system, an AI-only architecture, and a blockchain-only architecture. The evaluation considers behavioural detection performance, end-to-end latency, cost efficiency, throughput, reputation stability, tamper resistance, and component-wise ablation studies. Experimental results demonstrate that the hybrid architecture achieves higher behavioural fidelity and stronger trust guarantees than conventional reputation mechanisms while maintaining low per-ride blockchain cost and scalable operation through batched on-chain commitments.The primary contribution of this work is a sensor-driven credibility framework that transforms real-time behavioural evidence into a cryptographically verifiable trust primitive for ride-sharing ecosystems. By combining edge AI, IoT telemetry, and blockchain-based trust anchoring within a scalable hybrid architecture, Ridezy provides a practical foundation for trustworthy, transparent, and next-generation intelligent mobility systems.

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based automatic heuristic design (AHD) iteratively proposes and refines heuristics, pairing design rationales with executable code. Task-specific evaluators assess programs; execution outcomes and performance scores guide search. Many AHD systems keep the generator frozen; EvoTune and Co-Evolution of Algorithms and Language Model (CALM) instead update it from evaluated candidates. When such outcomes drive reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), they create a search-coupled loop: the evaluated candidate stream supplies both search-state updates and training signals for the model that generates future candidates. Yet validity and performance do not uniquely determine useful model updates; converting them into learning signals must account for the prompt and evolving search state that produced each candidate. We formulate online post-training of small open-weight LLMs in AHD as context-dependent signal construction and develop alternative mappings from program validity, task performance, and generation context to update signals. Using shared evaluated rollouts and matched update budgets, controlled experiments across AHD tasks and model families compare these mappings with online post-training baselines, testing their effects on validity, performance among valid proposals, and the yield of valid proposals that improve under contextual comparisons. Complementary checkpoint, frozen-search, and live-system evaluations assess whether proposal-level gains appear in updated checkpoint behavior and subsequent search, rather than arising solely from accumulated search state. A resource-matched comparison under pre-specified cost accounting tests whether online updating adds value beyond additional search with a frozen generator. Together, this design avoids treating end-to-end search gains alone as evidence of stronger heuristic-design capabilities.
